items.Sample_ID: HTH alloy X-750 noncharged CT specimens
Raw_Evidence_Span: The material used in this program was from 6.35 cm diameter alloy X-750 bars heat treated to the HTH condition with the composition provided in Table 1.
The noncharged testing used compact tension (CT) specimens that were 15.2 mm thick (B) with 20% side grooves (10% per side) and a width (W) of 30.5 mm.
The noncharged specimens were tested using an elastic-plastic fracture toughness testing technique at 25°C according to ASTM E813-89.

Processing.Process_Category: Wrought bar heat treatment and fracture toughness specimen preparation

Process_Text.original: 6.35 cm diameter alloy X-750 bars heat treated to the HTH condition. The HTH condition consists of a solution anneal at 1094°C for 1-2 h with a rapid air cool followed by aging at 704°C for 20 h. Noncharged CT specimens were 15.2 mm thick with 20% side grooves and 30.5 mm width; all specimens had an L-R orientation and were precracked at 30 Hz with final maximum K1 of 16.5 MPa√m.
Process_Text.simplified: X-750 bar was solution annealed, rapidly air cooled, aged, machined into L-R CT specimens with side grooves, fatigue precracked, and tested in air without hydrogen charging.

Structure_Text.original: The mean intercept grain size was 125 μm with small discrete M23C6 carbide precipitates decorating the grain boundaries. The alloy was strengthened by ~20 nm γ' precipitates with a rounded cuboidal shape and a weight fraction of 0.126. Primary carbides and carbonitrides, M(C, N), were observed to be aligned along the rolling direction.
Structure_Text.simplified: HTH X-750 contained 125 μm grains, grain-boundary M23C6 carbides, rounded cuboidal γ' strengthening precipitates, and primary carbides/carbonitrides aligned with the rolling direction.

Processing.Process_Category: Heat treated X-750, CT specimen machining, fatigue precracking, and hydrogen gas fracture toughness testing

Process_Text.original: CT specimens with a width (W) of 20.3 mm and thickness (B) of 10.1 mm were used. The specimens were fatigue precracked to an a/W of about 0.45 at a final maximum K1 of 16.5 MPa√m. All specimens were machined in an L-R orientation. At 54°C, the fracture tests were conducted on an electrohydraulic closed-loop machine in stroke control with a loading rate of 4.4 MPa√m/h. One specimen was tested at 0.44 MPa√m/h. Displacements were determined from an internal displacement gauge attached to the front face of the specimen and load from a system load cell. The autoclave was evacuated prior to adding the hydrogen gas.
Process_Text.simplified: HTH X-750 was machined into L-R CT specimens, fatigue precracked, placed in evacuated autoclave hydrogen gas, and tested for linear-elastic fracture toughness at 54°C under multiple hydrogen pressures.

Stage4.Process: hydrogen gas exposure during fracture testing

Structure_Text.original: Again, the fractography showed that all the specimens had an intergranular fracture morphology. At the low pressure, 0.14 MPa hydrogen, while the fractography shows a predominantly intergranular fracture, there is limited (less than 10%) transgranular faceted fracture. At a pressure of 0.34 and over, the fractography showed over 98% intergranular fracture.
Structure_Text.simplified: Hydrogen gas specimens fractured predominantly intergranularly; the 0.14 MPa specimen had less than 10% transgranular faceted fracture, while specimens at 0.34 MPa and above had over 98% intergranular fracture.

items.Sample_ID: HTH alloy X-750 bolt-loaded CT specimens with internal hydrogen and hydrogen environment
Raw_Evidence_Span: An additional test was performed on two bolt-loaded specimens to investigate the interaction of internal hydrogen and the hydrogen environment.
At this high pressure, the autoclave was held for four weeks. This allowed sufficient time for the specimens to achieve a uniform hydrogen concentration of 40 ppm.
The bolt-loaded specimens that were hydrogen charged and then tested in the hydrogen environment had a final stress intensity factor of 20 MPa√m for both specimens.

Processing.Process_Category: Bolt-loaded CT specimen hydrogen charging and hydrogen environment exposure

Process_Text.original: One specimen was loaded to a stress intensity factor of 22 MPa√m and the second was loaded to 33 MPa√m. The specimens were bolt loaded using a load transfer technique. The specimens were loaded to 98% of the final load in a tensile machine, then the load was transferred to the specimen by tightening the bolt while maintaining the crack mouth opening displacement constant as measured by a clip gage. After the bolt loading, the specimens were inserted into the autoclave, evacuated and then pressurized to 3.4 MPa and heated to 315°C. Once at temperature, the pressure was then increased to 21 MPa. At this high pressure, the autoclave was held for four weeks. The pressure was then kept constant, and the autoclave was cooled.
Process_Text.simplified: Two CT specimens were bolt loaded, transferred into an evacuated autoclave, exposed first to 3.4 MPa hydrogen while heating to 315°C, then to 21 MPa hydrogen for four weeks, cooled at constant pressure, removed, and evaluated by reverse load transfer.

Stage1.Load_Transfer: loaded to 98% of final load in a tensile machine, then bolt tightened while maintaining CMOD constant

items.Sample_ID: Critical grain-boundary hydrogen concentration model for HTH alloy X-750
Raw_Evidence_Span: A model based on a critical grain boundary hydrogen concentration is proposed to describe the behavior in both HEE and IHE conditions.
The best correlation between the grain boundary hydrogen concentration and the fracture toughness was achieved with a grain-boundary hydrogen trapping energy, HT, of 26 kJ/mol.
From the available data, the trapping energy could be estimated to be between 10 and 18 kJ/mol for the internally charged specimens.

Composition.Model_System: HTH alloy X-750 with hydrogen at grain boundaries and grain-boundary carbides

Process_Text.original: The trapped hydrogen concentration at the grain boundary may be described by Oriani's theory of trapping including the trapping at the grain boundary and grain boundary carbides. The local concentration is denoted here as CHσ because the matrix hydrogen solubility is increased ahead of a crack due to the hydrostatic stress field opening the lattice.
Process_Text.simplified: The model computes stress-modified matrix hydrogen concentration and trapped grain-boundary hydrogen concentration using Oriani trapping, Sievert solubility, crack-tip hydrostatic stress, and diffusion profiles.

Structure_Text.original: The trapping energy used to correlate the data is consistent with that determined by Young and Scully for trapping on the M23C6 grain boundary carbides in alloy 600. The characteristic distance for HEE is within two CTODs. This analysis results in a characteristic distance between 10 and 50 μm.
Structure_Text.simplified: The model links fracture to hydrogen trapping at grain boundaries and grain-boundary carbides, with a shorter HEE characteristic distance than IHE.

IHE_Tensile_Trapping_Energy.Original_Values: the trapping energy was determined to be 18 kJ/mol

Properties.Value: grain boundary hydrogen concentration controls embrittlement of HTH alloy X-750; HEE has shorter characteristic fracture distance and higher strain at fracture location than IHE
Properties.Original_Values: The degree of embrittlement of this alloy is controlled by the grain boundary hydrogen concentration irrespective of test temperature and bulk hydrogen concentration.
